Sulfoxaflor
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement set by JMPR and at EU level are substantially identical, since the ISO common name sulfoxaflor covers the two diastereomeric pairs of enantiomers of sulfoxaflor.
At EU level, the residue definition for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities is more comprehensive and includes the metabolite X11719474. X11719474 is a plant and soil metabolite, which has shown to be preferentially taken up by the roots of the plants and to be present (> LOQ) in the leafy parts of the crops in rotation crops, particularly in feed items.
The EU pesticide peer review considered metabolite X11719474 to be quantitatively relevant in primary and rotational crops (EFSA, 2014d). However, its inclusion in the residue definition for risk assessment of plant and animal products was provisional. Lacking toxicological data on the metabolite, currently exposure assessments are performed, assuming that this metabolite is as toxic as the parent compound.
The EU pesticides peer review agreed that if metabolite X11719474 is shown to be significantly less toxic than sulfoxaflor, the residue definition for the risk assessment should be revised to parent sulfoxaflor only.

efsa_comments:
The EU and JMPR enforcement residue definitions for plants are nearly identical, covering only parent fenazaquin. In the EU, for risk assessment, a second residue definition was established for metabolite TBPE. Overall, EU residue definitions for both enforcement and risk assessment for plants are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR derived a global enforcement residue definition. Furthermore, the risk assessment RD for plants derived by JMPR was not used for the risk assessment of pulses and leafy vegetables, as it was derived from metabolism studies in two crop groups (cereals and fruit). Hence requests for setting CXLs for pulses and mint were rejected.
For animals there is a slight difference in the residue definition for enforcement and RA, since EFSA is proposing fenazaquin only (for ruminants), while JMPR proposes a wider RD which includes also metabolites, i.e. tautomeric forms of 4‐hydroxyquinazoline (only for risk assessment) and 2‐hydroxy‐fenazaquin acid (for enforcement and risk assessment).
The RMS informed EFSA that during the renewal of the approval, the residue definitions for plant products (enforcement and risk assessment) are confirmed (still restricted to fruits). The previous tentative residue definition for leafy vegetables is no longer supported by the RMS.
The residue definitions for ruminants are also confirmed during the renewal, but the RMS highlighted that the representative uses do not include feed items and therefore they are not required.

JMPR:
Tetraniliprole
The residue is not fat soluble
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Tetraniliprole (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
Fat solubility not specified
efsa_comments:
The active substance was never assessed at the EU level – residue definitions have not been proposed at the EU level.
In the plant metabolism studies involving foliar applications (apples, potato, lettuce, paddy rice), soil drench application (tomato), granular in planting hole applications (rice) and seed treatments (potato and maize), in confined rotational crop metabolism studies and in processing studies, tetraniliprole was the major component (apple, tomato, lettuce, tomato, potato) of the radioactive residue. It was noted that apart from one outdoor study in maize and another in potatoes (seed treatment in furrow), all studies were conducted indoor. However, the JMPR concluded that the indoor studies sufficiently cover outdoor uses (since photodegradation was, at the most, only a minor path of degradation of tetraniliprole in soil).
Tetraniliprole is found in all primary crop commodities and is considered suitable as a marker compound. The JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.
Metabolite tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) was the only compound identified in relevant amounts in plant matrices. This metabolite was found at up to 20% TRR in tomato, rice grain and potatoes, but generally at levels ≤ 0.01 mg eq/kg in food commodities. This occurrence was confirmed in the supervised field trials, in which it was only found occasionally above the LOQ of 0.01 mg/kg, with tetraniliprole being present at levels about an order of magnitude higher.
Tetraniliprole is not stable under baking/brewing/boiling (pH 5, 100°C, 60 min) and sterilisation (pH 6, 120°C, 20 min) conditions. Under these conditions 65–68% and 1.1–1.5% AR was recovered as parent and 27–30% AR and 94% AR as tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), respectively. Processing under heating indicated conversion of parent tetraniliprole into tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), e.g. mustard greens (up to 20% TRR), broccoli (up to 29% TRR), tomato paste (23–48% TRR) and soya bean meal (up to 81% TRR).
The JMPR concluded that tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) may occur in primary and rotational crops and that the metabolite contributes significantly to the residue in processed commodities. Hence the JMPR agreed to define a residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities as tetraniliprole and tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359), expressed as tetraniliprole.
Metabolism in animals was assessed in goat and poultry studies. Tetraniliprole was a major component in all goat tissues (24–71% TRR), poultry fat (26–55% TRR) and eggs (4.2–14% TRR), but it contributes little to the overall residue in poultry muscle (3.7–10% TRR) and liver (1.6–4.2% TRR). Metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was a major compound in eggs and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg) and was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg). Parent tetraniliprole was also the major component in all cattle tissues and milk. Therefore, the JMPR decided to define the residue for compliance with the MRL as tetraniliprole.
In deciding which compound should be included in the residue definition for dietary risk assessment, the JMPR noted that the tetraniliprole was metabolised into numerous components, of which 17 were accounted for > 10% TRR and/or > 0.01 mg eq/kg.
The metabolites were considered in three categories, either covered by the toxicity of the parent, suitable for assessment by the TTC approach following Cramer Class III or by the TTC approach for genotoxic compounds.
Based on the assessment of metabolites, the JMPR proposed the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for animal commodities as follows: sum of tetraniliprole, tetraniliprole‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone (BSC‐CQ63359) and tetraniliprole‐benzylalcohol (BCS‐CZ91631), expressed as tetraniliprole.
EFSA does not fully agree on the residue definition for animal products. In particular, for poultry, parent tetraniliprole seems to be not a good marker substance and therefore the residue definition for enforcement is considered not appropriate.
In addition, tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone was found to be a the major compound in eggs (36% TRR, 0.030 mg eq/kg) and fat (63% TRR, 0.029 mg eq/kg); it was also found in liver (12% TRR, 0.065 mg eq/kg) and muscle (8.6% TRR, 0.001 mg eq/kg).
In the toxicological evaluation of 2021 JMPR, this metabolite (tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone) was reported to give alerts for genotoxicity using OECD QSAR ToolBox, Version 4.5.
In 2022, JMPR compared the exposure for this metabolite with the TTC Cramer class III threshold (see below JMPR risk assessment).
It is recommended to discuss with MS whether the proposed residue definitions for poultry are acceptable. Further details should also be checked in the JMPR evaluations, e.g. whether new information was available that allows to conclude that metabolite tetraniliprole‐despyridyl‐N‐methyl‐quinazolinone does not have genotoxicity alerts.

JMPR: Fluazaindolizine
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Fluazaindolizine (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
efsa_comments:
(a): This can be implemented by taking the maximum of the sum of compounds containing the imidazopyridine ring and hydrolysed using acid to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) or compounds containing the phenyl ring and hydrolysed to 8‐chloro‐6‐(trifluoromethyl)imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐2‐carboxylic acid (IN‐QEK31) (expressed as fluazaindolizine).
The metabolism of fluazaindolizine applied either as [phenyl‐14C(U)]fluazaindolizine (Ph‐14C) or [imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine‐5,8a‐14C]fluazaindolizine (IP‐5,8a‐14C) in plants was assessed in the following studies: in tomatoes, indoor, planting seedling into the soil treated by soil drenching at 1.5 kg a.s./ha and 30 days later with a soil direct application at 0.5 kg a.s./ha; in soya beans, seeds sown into soil treated with a drench application at 1 kg a.s./ha; in carrots, seeds sown into treated soil after a soil application of 1.5 kg a.s./ha, and a further application was done 30 days later at 0.5 kg a.s./ha; in potatoes, indoor, seeds sown into treated soil after a soil application of 1.0 kg a.s./ha, a further application was done 30 days later at 1.0 kg a.s./ha; mature sugarcane were transplanted into treated with soil drench application of 1.0 kg a.s./ha (JMPR 2022).
In the confined rotational crop study conducted in a glasshouse, bare sandy loam soil was treated with 14C‐fluazaindolizine at the equivalent of ≈ 1.95 kg a.s./ha (0.9× maximum seasonal rate) and spinach, radish and spring wheat were sown 30, 120 and 300 days after soil application (plant‐back interval, PBI). Fluazaindolizine, IN‐F4106 and IN‐QEK31 were the major residues extracted from soil.
Regarding the residue definition for enforcement in plants, as fluazaindolizine occurs in most crops that have detectable residues a pragmatic option as analysis of other compounds involves an intensive hydrolysis step, the JMPR decided the residue definition for compliance with MRLs in plants should be fluazaindolizine.
Regarding the residue definition for risk assessment for plant commodities the JMPR considered the likely occurrence of the compounds and the toxicological properties of the candidates. Compounds considered were fluazaindolizine, IN‐REG72, IN‐A5760, INF4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54 and their conjugates. Each of the compounds is variously the predominant or a significant residue in primary and rotated crops. The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities should account for residues of fluazaindolizine, and free and conjugated forms of the following compounds: IN‐REG72, IN‐QEK31, IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33 and IN‐TMQ01.
It was noted that the analytical method utilising acid hydrolysis converts conjugates to their free form and also hydrolyses fluazaindolizine to IN‐QEK31 and IN‐F4106, IN‐REG72 to IN‐QEK31 and IN‐A5760 and converts IN‐RYC33 to IN‐QEK31. To avoid double counting when expressing all residues in terms of fluazaindolizine, the JMPR considered the maximum of the sum of IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 or IN‐QEK31 measured after hydrolysis to provide the best measure of the compounds included in the residue definition.
To derive the input values according to the residue definition for dietary risk assessment proposed for plant commodities, JMPR added to the residue concentration of parent compound the maximum concentration of either the sum of compounds containing the imidazopyridine ring and hydrolysed using acid to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) or the compounds containing the phenyl ring and hydrolysed to IN‐QEK31 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) were used. The information provided in the JMPR report however is not sufficiently detailed to provide comments whether the approach used by JMPR and the derived risk assessment values are appropriate.
In addition, a field rotational crop study was assessed by the JMPR, and it was concluded that, at the maximum use pattern considered by the JMPR, soil application at up to 2.24 kg a.s./ha, residues of fluazaindolizine and metabolites are expected in rotational crops.
JMPR assessed studies on the metabolism of fluazaindolizine labelled on [Ph‐14C(U)]‐fluazaindolizine and [imidazo‐(1,2‐α)‐pyridine‐2‐14C]‐fluazaindolizine in lactating goats and laying hens and separate studies following dosing with metabolites IN‐QEK31 (lactating goats, laying hens) and IN‐QZY47 (lactating goats) and IN‐TMQ01 (lactating goats).
Regarding the residue definition for enforcement for animal commodities, fluazaindolizine was present in milk, eggs and all tissues in the lactating goat and most tissues in laying hen metabolism studies and would be suitable for monitoring compliance. Thus, the JMPR decided the residue definition for compliance with MRLs in livestock should be fluazaindolizine.
In deciding which compounds should be included in the residue definition for risk assessment for animal commodities, JMPR considered the likely occurrence of the compounds and the toxicological properties of the candidates. The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for risk assessment for animal commodities should be the sum of fluazaindolizine, IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine).
The residue definition for enforcement derived by the JMPR is the same as the residue definition in the EU (by default, parent only). Since the substance was never assessed in the EU there is no RD‐RA established at the EU level.
Overall, based on the information provided in the JMPR report, EFSA would tend to disagree on the proposed residue definitions:
As regards the residue definition for plants (MRL enforcement), the parent compound is considered not an appropriate marker substance, since parent compound was only a minor component of the residue.
In animal products, the livestock metabolism studies showed that parent compound is transferred to animal matrices; however, considering that parent compound is only a minor component of the residues in feed, it might not be a relevant marker compound for MRL enforcement in animal matrices.
The residue definition for animal matrices relevant for risk assessment should also better reflect the expected residues resulting from the intake of fluazaindolizine related residues (metabolites in feed items).
For the risk assessment residue definition (plant matrices), JMPR proposed a new approach, including metabolites and/or hydrolysis products generated under the drastic conditions applied in the analytical methods used to analyse the samples, where degradation products of both ring systems were produced. To derive the risk assessment values, the maximum of the two groups of metabolites containing either the benzene‐ring or the imidazo‐pyridine‐ring system should be taken into account.
Since there is only limited experience on this approach, EFSA would need to verify the details of the assessment. Hence, it is proposed to await the publication of the JMPR evaluation, to perform a more detailed assessment and conclude on the appropriateness of the residue definitions proposed by JMPR.
As the assessment of this substance is ongoing at EU level, proposals for EU residue definitions are expected to be presented by the RMS which will be further discussed by MS experts in due course.

Compounds considered were fluazaindolizine, IN‐REG72, IN‐A5760, INF4106, IN‐QEK31, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33, IN‐TMQ01, IN‐UJV12 and IN‐TQD54 and their conjugates. Each of the compounds is variously the predominant or a significant residue in primary and rotated crops. The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for dietary risk assessment for plant commodities should account for residues of fluazaindolizine, and free and conjugated forms of the following compounds: IN‐REG72, IN‐QEK31, IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47, IN‐RYC33 and IN‐TMQ01.
It was noted that the analytical method utilising acid hydrolysis converts conjugates to their free form and also hydrolyses fluazaindolizine to IN‐QEK31 and IN‐F4106, IN‐REG72 to IN‐QEK31 and IN‐A5760 and converts IN‐RYC33 to IN‐QEK31. To avoid double counting when expressing all residues in terms of fluazaindolizine, the JMPR considered the maximum of the sum of IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 or IN‐QEK31 measured after hydrolysis to provide the best measure of the compounds included in the residue definition.
To derive the input values according to the residue definition for dietary risk assessment proposed for plant commodities, JMPR added to the residue concentration of parent compound the maximum concentration of either the sum of compounds containing the imidazopyridine ring and hydrolysed using acid to IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106, IN‐QZY47 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) or the compounds containing the phenyl ring and hydrolysed to IN‐QEK31 (expressed as fluazaindolizine) were used. The information provided in the JMPR report however is not sufficiently detailed to provide comments whether the approach used by JMPR and the derived risk assessment values are appropriate.
In addition, a field rotational crop study was assessed by the JMPR, and it was concluded that, at the maximum use pattern considered by the JMPR, soil application at up to 2.24 kg a.s./ha, residues of fluazaindolizine and metabolites are expected in rotational crops.
JMPR assessed studies on the metabolism of fluazaindolizine labelled on [Ph‐14C(U)]‐fluazaindolizine and [imidazo‐(1,2‐α)‐pyridine‐2‐14C]‐fluazaindolizine in lactating goats and laying hens and separate studies following dosing with metabolites IN‐QEK31 (lactating goats, laying hens) and IN‐QZY47 (lactating goats) and IN‐TMQ01 (lactating goats).
Regarding the residue definition for enforcement for animal commodities, fluazaindolizine was present in milk, eggs and all tissues in the lactating goat and most tissues in laying hen metabolism studies and would be suitable for monitoring compliance. Thus, the JMPR decided the residue definition for compliance with MRLs in livestock should be fluazaindolizine.
In deciding which compounds should be included in the residue definition for risk assessment for animal commodities, JMPR considered the likely occurrence of the compounds and the toxicological properties of the candidates. The JMPR agreed that the residue definition for risk assessment for animal commodities should be the sum of fluazaindolizine, IN‐A5760, IN‐F4106 and IN‐TMQ01 (expressed as fluazaindolizine).
The residue definition for enforcement derived by the JMPR is the same as the residue definition in the EU (by default, parent only). Since the substance was never assessed in the EU there is no RD‐RA established at the EU level.
Overall, based on the information provided in the JMPR report, EFSA would tend to disagree on the proposed residue definitions:
As regards the residue definition for plants (MRL enforcement), the parent compound is considered not an appropriate marker substance, since parent compound was only a minor component of the residue.
In animal products, the livestock metabolism studies showed that parent compound is transferred to animal matrices; however, considering that parent compound is only a minor component of the residues in feed, it might not be a relevant marker compound for MRL enforcement in animal matrices.
The residue definition for animal matrices relevant for risk assessment should also better reflect the expected residues resulting from the intake of fluazaindolizine related residues (metabolites in feed items).
For the risk assessment residue definition (plant matrices), JMPR proposed a new approach, including metabolites and/or hydrolysis products generated under the drastic conditions applied in the analytical methods used to analyse the samples, where degradation products of both ring systems were produced. To derive the risk assessment values, the maximum of the two groups of metabolites containing either the benzene‐ring or the imidazo‐pyridine‐ring system should be taken into account.
Since there is only limited experience on this approach, EFSA would need to verify the details of the assessment. Hence, it is proposed to await the publication of the JMPR evaluation, to perform a more detailed assessment and conclude on the appropriateness of the residue definitions proposed by JMPR.
As the assessment of this substance is ongoing at EU level, proposals for EU residue definitions are expected to be presented by the RMS which will be further discussed by MS experts in due course.
